name: Oden (Japanese Fish Cake & Daikon Simmer)
why: Oden is Japan's classic cold-weather pot — daikon, konnyaku and fish cakes quietly soaking up flavour in a clean dashi-soy broth for hours. It's the ultimate low-effort autumn dinner: assemble it, simmer it gently, and the broth does the work. Perfect comfort food as the nights get properly cold.
author: Henry
ingredients: 750g oden set (assorted Japanese fish cakes & fish balls)
184g atsuage (firm deep-fried tofu cutlet), cut into strips
4 dried knotted kombu (or knot up rehydrated strips)
1.4L (6 cups) strong dashi (use a dashi packet/powder for depth)
2 tbsp usukuchi (light) soy sauce (or regular, broth will be darker)

steps: Peel the daikon, slice into 1cm rounds, and shave the sharp outer edges flat with a knife so the slices sit flat in the pot.
Score one face of the konnyaku in a shallow crosshatch (3mm deep) to help it absorb the broth.
Blanch the oden fish cakes (nerimono) and the atsuage in boiling water for 15-30 seconds to draw off excess oil, then drain and rinse the pot.
Combine the dashi, light soy sauce, sake, mirin and salt in the pot and stir to mix.
Add the daikon, konnyaku, knotted kombu and hard-boiled eggs. Bring to a boil, then drop the heat to the lowest simmer.
Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes — the daikon should be just tender but still holding its shape.

Cut the larger fish cakes into bite-sized pieces and add them to the pot with the atsuage. Continue simmering gently for a further 15-20 minutes, topping up with water if the level drops, so the fish cakes soak up the broth.
Ladle the oden and its broth into bowls (or serve it family-style straight from the pot).
Serve hot with a small dish of karashi mustard on the side, mixed with a little mirin or broth to taste.

pro_tips: The broth is the whole game — use the strongest dashi you have (a proper dashi packet or kelp + katsuobushi, not a weak powder) and balance it with light soy, sake and mirin. A good oden broth should be clear and intensely savoury, not dark.

Oden improves overnight: the ingredients keep absorbing flavour as they sit. If you have time, assemble it, give it a base simmer, then refrigerate and reheat gently before serving — that's how it's traditionally eaten in winter.
